title: Workers' Compensation and Construction Payroll: What Belongs on Every Pay Run
summary: How workers' compensation connects to construction payroll. Covers class codes, experience mods, premium calculations, and what to get right on every pay run.
body_markdown:
Workers' comp is not a line item you set and forget. In construction, your payroll data directly determines what you pay in premiums. Every dollar of reported wages, every class code assignment, every hour logged feeds into a calculation your carrier audits at the end of the policy year. Get the payroll wrong, and you either overpay all year or get hit with a lump-sum adjustment at audit.


For trade contractors running crews across[multiple states](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/multi-state-payroll-construction-guide) and project types, workers' comp adds a layer of complexity that generic payroll systems aren't built to handle. This guide covers how premiums connect to payroll, where contractors lose money, and what your pay run needs to include to keep premiums accurate and audits clean.


## **How Workers' Comp Premiums Are Calculated**


The basic formula is straightforward:


**Class Code Rate x Experience Modification Rate x (Payroll / $100) = Premium**


Each piece comes from a different place, and each one is affected by what happens in your[payroll system](https://www.buildtrayd.com/products/payroll/construction-payroll) .


### **Class Codes**


Every employee is assigned a class code based on the type of work they perform. Codes are set by the NCCI in most states, though some states maintain their own rating bureaus. Higher-risk work carries higher rates. A carpenter has a different rate than an electrician, and both are significantly higher than clerical office staff.


In construction, workers frequently shift between tasks and trades. That's where classification gets complicated.


### **Experience Modification Rate (EMR)**


Your EMR compares your claims history to similar businesses in your class code. A mod of 1.0 is the industry average. Below 1.0 means fewer or smaller claims, which lowers your premium. Above 1.0 raises it.


The mod uses roughly three years of payroll and claims data. That means today's[payroll reports](https://www.buildtrayd.com/products/payroll/construction-payroll-reports) are shaping your premium two to three years from now.


### **Payroll**


Carriers estimate your annual payroll at the start of the policy. At year-end (or more frequently with pay-as-you-go plans), they audit actual payroll against the estimate. Higher actual payroll means you owe the difference. Lower means a credit.


The numbers your carrier audits come directly from your payroll records. If those records are messy, the audit will be too.


## **Where Construction Contractors Lose Money on Workers' Comp**


Most overpayment isn't the result of high claim rates. It's the result of bad data.


### **Misclassified Workers**


This is the most common and most expensive mistake. A project manager doing office work gets coded as a field laborer. A GC's crew gets lumped under a single high-risk code instead of being split by actual duties. Clerical staff who never visit a jobsite carry the same rate as the crew pouring concrete.


Every misclassification means you're paying a premium for risk that doesn't exist.


### **Overtime Reported Incorrectly**


Most states require workers' comp premiums to be calculated on base wages only, not the overtime premium (the extra half of time-and-a-half). If your payroll system reports gross wages including the overtime multiplier without separating the base component, you're overstating the payroll figure your carrier uses. For contractors running[prevailing wage jobs](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/what-is-prevailing-wage-davis-bacon-guide) with significant[overtime](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/construction-overtime-rules-federal-state-prevailing-wage) , this is a material dollar amount.


### **Subcontractor Insurance Gaps**


If a sub on your project doesn't carry their own workers' comp policy, their payroll gets added to yours for premium calculation. Your carrier will pick this up at audit. The fix is verifying certificates of insurance before subs start work and keeping those records current.


### **Stale Payroll Estimates**


Contractors whose workforce fluctuates seasonally often start the policy year with an estimate based on peak headcount. If actual payroll comes in lower, they've been overpaying premiums all year and don't recoup the difference until the audit settles. Pay-as-you-go plans calculate premiums each pay period based on actual wages, but only work if the payroll data feeding them is accurate.


## **What Belongs on Every Pay Run**


Getting workers' comp right isn't a separate process from payroll. It's built into payroll, if your system supports it.


### **Accurate Hours by Worker and Classification**


Every worker's hours need to be recorded against the correct class code. If a worker splits time between field work and shop fabrication, those hours should be reported separately. Your[foreman app](https://www.buildtrayd.com/products/field/foreman-app) or time tracking system is the first link in this chain.


### **Base Wage Separation**


Overtime premiums, shift differentials, and certain bonuses are typically excluded from workers' comp payroll. Your system should separate base wages from these components automatically, not rely on someone doing the math afterward.


### **Subcontractor Verification Records**


Every sub on a project should have a current certificate of insurance on file before they start. If their coverage lapses mid-project, your exposure increases. Tracking this alongside payroll is part of your total[compliance picture](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/pre-bid-compliance-checklist-public-works-contractors) .


### **Per-Project Cost Allocation**


Workers' comp is a labor cost, and it needs to land on the right job. If your payroll system ties comp costs to specific projects, your[job costing](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/construction-payroll-vs-regular-payroll) reflects actual burden instead of a blended average that hides which projects are profitable.

## **FAQs**


### How are workers' comp premiums calculated in construction?


Premiums use three factors: the class code rate for the work performed, your experience modification rate (EMR), and total payroll. The formula is Class Code Rate x EMR x (Payroll / $100). All three are affected by payroll accuracy.


### What is an experience modification rate?


Your EMR compares your company's workers' comp claims history to similar businesses in your industry. A rate below 1.0 lowers your premium. A rate above 1.0 raises it. The calculation uses roughly three years of payroll and claims data.


### Why do workers' comp class codes matter for construction payroll?


Each class code carries a different premium rate based on injury risk. Misclassifying workers (coding office staff at field laborer rates, for example) means you pay for risk that doesn't exist. Accurate classification directly affects what you spend.


### What payroll data do workers' comp carriers audit?


Carriers audit total payroll by class code, overtime breakdowns (base vs. premium pay), subcontractor insurance records, and employee classifications. Incomplete records lead to audit adjustments that can mean significant additional charges.


### What is pay-as-you-go workers' comp?


Pay-as-you-go plans calculate your premium each pay period based on actual payroll instead of an annual estimate. This prevents large year-end audit adjustments and improves cash flow, but it requires your payroll system to report accurate wages by class code every pay cycle.


*This guide is for informational purposes only. Workers' compensation requirements, class codes, and premium calculations vary by state and carrier. Consult your insurance broker or state workers' compensation board for requirements specific to your situation.*
